narrative.text: One of three miniature learning-curve plots embedded inside Figure 4.1, the chapter's framework schematic ("In phase 1 (left), the learning..."). It shows five coloured curves rising from 0 and flattening by roughly x=20 on an unlabelled 0-50 horizontal axis against a 0.0-1.0 vertical one: an orange curve settling near 0.97, red and green both near 0.62 (green rising more slowly and crossing red at about x=27), blue near 0.46 and purple near 0.33. No axis titles, legend or tick labels beyond the numbers — it is an illustration of the SHAPE of a learning curve inside the diagram, not a figure to be read for values.

narrative.text: A second miniature learning-curve plot inside Figure 4.1, placed at two points in the schematic. Five curves on the same unlabelled 0-50 by 0.0-1.0 axes: red highest and flat near 0.75 from about x=7, orange and green together near 0.48-0.50, purple just below at about 0.43, and blue lowest at about 0.25. Same role as the other two thumbnails — illustrative, not quantitative.

narrative.text: The third miniature learning-curve plot inside Figure 4.1. Blue is highest and flattens fastest, near 0.90 by x=7; green settles near 0.70; orange plateaus low near 0.20; and red and purple both keep climbing across the whole range to meet around 0.42 at x=50 — the only one of the three thumbnails in which two curves have not converged by the right-hand edge. Illustrative, not quantitative.

basis.saw: a six-series line chart with shaded confidence bands, x-axis alpha

narrative.text: Figure 4.4: "Sensitivity of PTRRα to α on selected LCDB instances (T = 44, k = 22)". Normalised cumulative reward (ALG/OPT) against α from 0.1 to 1.0, six datasets, each a line with a shaded 95% band. The reading the figure is for is that the datasets DISAGREE about α: ds 55 is flat at about 0.995 throughout, ds 67 RISES with α (0.943 to 0.954), ds 16 peaks in the middle around 0.846 at α≈0.4-0.7, while ds 58 (0.907 to 0.886), ds 19 (0.789 to 0.722) and ds 46 (0.735 to 0.696) all FALL. Every curve's total variation across the sweep is small — the largest, ds 19, moves about 0.067 — so the sensitivity is real but shallow, and the bands of ds 19 and ds 46 overlap over much of the range.

basis.saw: three side-by-side line panels, many unlabelled curves each, shared y-axis

narrative.text: Figure 4.5: mean LCDB reward curves for three datasets whose best α on the grid differs — Dataset 19 (best α = 0.1), Dataset 16 (best α = 0.7) and Dataset 67 (best α = 1.0). Each panel plots reward = 1 − error_rate against pull count (anchor index) from 0 to about 44, with one coloured curve per arm and no legend. The panels look different in exactly the way the caption's framing implies: Dataset 19's curves are still climbing and widely spread at the right-hand edge (roughly 0.25 to 0.85); Dataset 16's are tighter and mostly flattening (about 0.55 to 0.93); Dataset 67's jump almost immediately to a dense band near 0.9-0.97 with three visible stragglers at about 0.73, 0.64 and 0.60. Placed twice on the page.

basis.saw: a two-series line chart with error bars, subsidy vs no subsidy

narrative.text: Figure 6.1: "Impact of Financial Supplement on Finding Correct Cascade with Supplement, 100 agents". Proportion of correct cascades against signal strength from 0.5 to 1.0. The orange "our subsidy" curve starts at about 0.89 at signal strength 0.5 and reaches 1.0 by 0.6, staying there; the blue "no subsidy" curve starts at about 0.51 and climbs through roughly 0.70 at 0.6, 0.85 at 0.7 and 0.94 at 0.8 before meeting 1.0 near 0.9. The gap is largest at the weakest signal and closed by 0.9, which is the claim: the subsidy matters precisely where signals are weak.

basis.saw: a three-series line chart, population sizes 10/100/1000, no subsidy

narrative.text: Figure 6.2: "Probability of Finding Correct Cascade without Supplement", for 10, 100 and 1000 agents. All three curves lie on top of one another within their error bars — about 0.50 at signal strength 0.5, 0.67 at 0.6, 0.80 at 0.7, 0.93 at 0.8, and 1.0 by 0.9 — so the figure's content is a NEGATIVE: without the supplement, population size makes no visible difference to the chance of a correct cascade. Read against Figure 6.1, that is what isolates the subsidy as the cause there.

basis.saw: a six-series line chart with error bars, subsidy per agent index

narrative.text: Figure 6.3: "Average Subsidy Progression for 100 Agents", one curve per signal strength. The curves separate by how long the subsidy has to keep paying. At signal strength 0.99 (yellow) and 0.9 (magenta) the subsidy is at or near zero throughout. At 0.8 (cyan) it spikes early and is gone by about agent 18; at 0.7 (red) it peaks near 0.07 at about agent 4 and decays to zero by about agent 60; at 0.6 (green) it peaks near 0.062 around agent 8 and is still decaying, at about 0.003, at agent 100. At 0.51 (blue) it behaves differently in kind — it RISES to about 0.022 by agent 40 and then stays flat to agent 100 rather than decaying. The weakest signal is the one where the subsidy never stops being needed.

basis.saw: a 4x3 table of formulae with graded green shading

narrative.text: Figure 7.1, which the caption itself calls a table: the reward the agents of Section 7.3.2 receive as a function of where the true threshold θ falls. Columns are Agent A, Agent B and Agent C; rows are the four cases θ < s_A, s_A ≤ θ < s_B, s_B ≤ θ < s_C, and s_C ≤ θ. A cell is either the quadratic (α/2)(T−θ)² — dark green, the un-switched payoff — or the square root √(2T/α̃_X) for that agent, in progressively paler green. The shading tracks the staircase: the top row is all quadratic, and each row down converts one more agent, left to right, so the bottom row is all square roots. The colour carries no quantity beyond that ordering.

basis.saw: a two-series line chart, switch point against prior standard deviation

narrative.text: Figure 7.2: "Switch point as a function of standard deviation σ for prior of N(25, σ²)". The blue "switches" curve starts at 25 when σ is near 0 — coinciding with the flat orange μ = 25 reference line — rises steeply to about 70 by σ = 20, then flattens, reaching roughly 80 by σ = 40 and about 82 at σ = 100, with visible small steps in the upper range where the switch point moves by discrete amounts. The two lines meet only at the left-hand edge: the more uncertain the prior, the later the switch, but with sharply diminishing effect.

basis.saw: an alpha sweep over datasets 0-25, nine series with 95% bands

narrative.text: Figure B.1, first of three panels: alpha sweeps with 95% t-intervals for LCDB datasets 0-25 (T = 44, k = 22) — the appendix's full-corpus version of Figure 4.4. Nine datasets, normalised cumulative reward against α from 0.1 to 1.0. Most are close to flat between 0.84 and 0.94; ds 19 (pink) is the clear outlier, falling from 0.789 to 0.722 across the sweep and sitting about 0.09 below the next lowest. ds 25 leads at about 0.938 falling gently to 0.928; ds 12 and ds 16 rise slightly; ds 9 and ds 17 fall away after about α = 0.6.

basis.saw: an alpha sweep over datasets 28-50, nine series with 95% bands

narrative.text: Figure B.1, second panel: datasets 28-50 on the same axes. ds 42 is highest and almost perfectly flat at about 0.955; ds 32, ds 50 and ds 33 cluster near 0.91-0.92; ds 28, ds 30 and ds 49 sit around 0.89-0.91 with ds 49 rising slightly; ds 41 is flat at 0.866 until about α = 0.8 then falls to 0.857. ds 46 (pink) is the outlier here, falling steadily from 0.735 to 0.696 — the same shape ds 19 has in the first panel.

basis.saw: an alpha sweep over datasets 51-71, nine series with 95% bands

narrative.text: Figure B.1, third panel: datasets 51-71. The tightest of the three — every curve lies between 0.885 and 1.0, with no outlier of the ds 19 / ds 46 kind. ds 55 is flat at about 0.995, ds 51 flat at 0.958. ds 67 rises from 0.943 to about 0.955 and ds 63 rises then falls back to 0.926; ds 58 falls from 0.908 to 0.885 and ds 71 from 0.903 to 0.889. Across all three panels the pattern is that a few datasets are α-sensitive in opposite directions and most are nearly flat, which is what makes a single global α defensible and a per-dataset one better.

basis.saw: a two-series line chart with error bars, 10 agents

narrative.text: Figure C.1: "Proportion Correct Cascades for 10 Agents" — the small-population version of Figure 6.1. The orange "our subsidy" and blue "no subsidy" curves are nearly on top of each other, orange only slightly above: about 0.53 against 0.49 at signal strength 0.5, 0.67 against 0.63 at 0.6, 0.85 against 0.80 at 0.7, and both at 1.0 by 0.9, with overlapping error bars throughout. With ten agents the subsidy buys almost nothing.

basis.saw: a two-series line chart with error bars, 1000 agents

narrative.text: Figure C.2: "Proportion Correct Cascades for 1000 Agents". The same pair at the large-population end, and the separation is at its widest: "our subsidy" is already at about 0.98 at signal strength 0.5 and at 1.0 from 0.6 onward, while "no subsidy" starts at about 0.53 and climbs through 0.70, 0.87 and 0.95 before converging near 0.9. Set beside Figure C.1 and Figure 6.1 (100 agents), the three make one point the individual figures do not: the subsidy's benefit GROWS with population size.

basis.saw: a six-series line chart with error bars, 10 agents, subsidy per agent

narrative.text: Figure C.3: "Average Subsidy Progression for 10 Agents". With only ten agents the curves are jagged rather than smooth: red (0.7) oscillates between about 0.03 and 0.083 with no clear decay, green (0.6) between 0.03 and 0.054, cyan (0.8) spikes to 0.061 at agent 2 and decays erratically to near zero by agent 8, magenta (0.9) peaks at 0.024 and fades, blue (0.51) creeps up to about 0.012, and yellow (0.99) is flat at zero. The decay-to-zero structure visible at 100 and 1000 agents is not resolvable at this population size.

basis.saw: a six-series line chart with dense error bars, 1000 agents

narrative.text: Figure C.4: "Average Subsidy Progression for 1000 Agents". The clearest of the three subsidy figures. Cyan (0.8), magenta (0.9) and red (0.7) all spike in the first few agents and are at zero within roughly 10, 10 and 40 agents; green (0.6) peaks near 0.075 and decays to zero by about agent 130; yellow (0.99) never leaves zero. Blue (0.51) again behaves differently in kind — it rises to about 0.022 by agent 100 and then decays very slowly, still paying about 0.011 at agent 1000. The error bars are dense enough to read as a band. Same qualitative story as Figure 6.3 at 100 agents, with the slow decay of the weakest-signal curve now visible over a longer horizon.
